title: Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:29–40)
hookLine: a rash vow ends in tragedy, and the rabbis condemn it

lines: THE SPIRIT IS ALREADY ON HIM.
cards: Jephthah's brothers drove him out of the house; his mother wasn't their mother. Years later, with the Ammonites at war with Israel, the elders of Gilead come and ask him to lead them. He agrees.
The spirit of the Lord comes upon him, the text says. He already has what he needs. Then, on the way to battle, he adds something nobody asked for.
A vow. Whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace, shall be the Lord's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.

teach.h: OUT OF THE DOORS: HIS ONLY CHILD.
teach.b: He wins, and comes home to Mizpah. Out of the doors comes his daughter, dancing, with timbrels. She was his only child.

"I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back." She answers with strange steadiness: do to me what you said. She asks for time to go up into the mountains with her friends and mourn, and he lets her go.
When she returns, the text says only that he did with her according to his vow, and that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament her. She is never named. The rabbis do not admire this.
The Talmud names Jephthah among those who asked improperly: what if the thing that came out of the house had been unfit for an offering? A midrash goes further.
The vow could have been released; Phinehas the priest was alive then. But Jephthah said, I'm the leader, why should I go to him? And Phinehas said, I'm the high priest, why should I go to him?

teach.h: TWO PROUD MEN, A GIRL LOST.
teach.b: Between two proud men, a girl was lost. Later commentators even differ on what happened to her: some read the verse as it sounds; some read it as a life set apart. Either way, the rabbis draw the same lesson.
A promise made in a rush of feeling, to make sure of something already given, can cost what no one meant to pay.

how: Jews study Jephthah's vow with the Talmud and midrash beside the text; the rabbinic tradition treats the vow as rash and wrong, and Jewish law has ways for a vow to be released before a sage or court.

o: a promise made in haste that cost him his only child
a peace treaty sworn with the Ammonite king
an oath of loyalty the elders of Gilead swore

games.q: rash vows cost — tap the pairs.
p: vowed whatever came out of his doors
could have released the vow, says a midrash

s: the rabbis praise Jephthah for keeping his word
the Talmud lists him among those who asked improperly, and a midrash blames pride for the girl's loss.
the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament Jephthah's daughter
the text says so at the end of Judges 11.
the text tells us the daughter's name

games.q: you're Jephthah. you've come home in victory, and your only child walks out of the door to meet you. what do you say?
o: I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back.
I'll go to the priest and ask for the vow to be released.
say nothing, and hope it passes.
games.why: he says he cannot go back. a midrash says the vow could have been released, but neither Jephthah nor Phinehas the priest would go to the other.

practice: Think of the promises that come out of you quickly, sure, no problem, I'll never do that again, and pick one you've made lately. Look for the gap between the feeling and the words, and let it be one breath longer next time.
If there's one you can't keep well, notice who you could talk to.

wordCard.voice: Jephthah's vow. Made in haste, when the spirit of the Lord was already on him, and kept at a terrible cost.

orig.note: Hebrew: a vow, a promise made to God, the word for what Jephthah vowed in Judges 11:30.

carryVoice: Your line: rash vows cost. Deborah's song, the mother at the window, mighty while hiding, the fleece, three hundred, the bramble, and a vow: that was the week. Seven days, done.

sources.q: I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back.
